query: For high-entropy alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict the observations relative to a baseline, state the limits within which the hypothesis should hold, identify evidence that would support it, and specify an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In single-phase high-entropy alloys, the observed enhanced hardness and strength arise from a deformation‐induced local transformation at grain boundaries that creates ultra-fine, amorphous (or highly disordered) interfacial layers while also promoting short-range chemical ordering. This dynamic transformation, activated at nanocrystalline grain sizes (i.e. in the inverse Hall–Petch regime), both impedes dislocation motion and refines the microstructure, thereby increasing yield strength and hardness relative to coarse-grained samples.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, equiatomic high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) in a coarse-grained, well-annealed state.
generation.intervention: Apply controlled severe plastic deformation (or a similar strain-inducing process) to refine the grain structure to the nanocrystalline regime under inert conditions.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted at room temperature in an inert environment to minimize oxidation effects; samples compared between untreated (coarse-grained) and deformed (nanocrystalline) states.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of ultra-nanocrystalline, partially amorphized grain boundary layers and/or nanoclusters of short-range chemical order.
generation.mechanism: Under high-strain conditions, local stress concentrations at grain boundaries trigger a dynamic transformation (partial amorphization) that creates ultra-fine interfacial regions. These regions, potentially stabilized by short-range chemical ordering, act as effective barriers to dislocation motion and increase resistance to shear, resulting in higher hardness and yield strength. The underlying dislocation behavior is modified both at the core and at the boundaries, leading to an inverse Hall–Petch-like effect.
generation.predicted_outcome: The nanocrystalline (and partially amorphized/ordered) samples will exhibit significantly higher hardness and yield strength compared to the untreated, coarse-grained baseline. Microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM) should reveal the presence of ultra-fine grain boundaries with indications of amorphous or short-range ordered structures.
generation.baseline: Coarse-grained high-entropy alloy samples without severe plastic deformation or induced nanostructuring.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold in single-phase, near-equiatomic high-entropy alloys under conditions where the grain size is refined into the nanocrystalline regime (typically below ~100 nm) and in environments where extrinsic factors (e.g., oxidation) do not interfere. Its applicability to multiphase systems or alloys with distinctly different chemistries is uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: There remains uncertainty in quantifying the exact degree of amorphization and the role of short-range ordering under different deformation conditions. The interplay between dislocation dynamics and chemical ordering in controlling the hardness and strength needs further quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of a single-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi): one set in the coarse-grained state (baseline) and a second set subjected to controlled severe plastic deformation to achieve nanocrystalline grain sizes. Characterize both sets using TEM to analyze grain boundary structures, determine the presence and extent of any amorphous or short-range ordered interfacial layers, and perform nanoindentation or microcompression tests to measure hardness and yield strength.
measurements: Microstructural analysis via high-resolution TEM (to detect amorphous or disordered grain boundary layers)
Nanoindentation or microcompression testing for hardness and yield strength
Grain size distribution from EBSD or STEM
Chemical mapping (e.g., via APT or EDS) to assess short-range order
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the deformed, nanocrystalline samples do not exhibit the formation of amorphous or highly disordered grain boundary layers (or any significant increase in short-range chemical ordering) and do not demonstrate a statistically significant increase in hardness and yield strength compared to the coarse-grained baseline, then the hypothesis that local dynamic transformations mediate strengthening in these HEAs is falsified.

Electronic descriptors for dislocation deformation behavior and intrinsic ductility in bcc high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractControlling the balance between strength and damage tolerance in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) is central to their application as structural materials. Materials discovery efforts for HEAs are therefore impeded by an incomplete understanding of the chemical factors governing this balance. Through first-principles calculations, this study explores factors governing intrinsic ductility of a crucial subset of HEAs—those with a body-centered cubic (bcc) crystal structure. Analyses of three sets of bcc HEAs comprising nine different compositions reveal that alloy chemistry profoundly influences screw dislocation core structure, dislocation vibrational properties, and intrinsic ductility parameters derived from unstable stacking fault and surface energies. Key features in the electronic structure are identified that correlate with these properties: the fraction of occupied bonding states and bimodality of the d-orbital density of states. Nanoscale origins of the damage tolerance of the high-entropy alloy CrMnFeCoNi

Abstract: AbstractDamage tolerance can be an elusive characteristic of structural materials requiring both high strength and ductility, properties that are often mutually exclusive. High-entropy alloys are of interest in this regard. Specifically, the single-phase CrMnFeCoNi alloy displays tensile strength levels of ∼1 GPa, excellent ductility (∼60–70%) and exceptional fracture toughness (KJIc>200 MPa√m). Here through the use of in situ straining in an aberration-corrected transmission electron microscope, we report on the salient atomistic to micro-scale mechanisms underlying the origin of these properties. We identify a synergy of multiple deformation mechanisms, rarely achieved in metallic alloys, which generates high strength, work hardening and ductility, including the easy motion of Shockley partials, their interactions to form stacking-fault parallelepipeds, and arrest at planar slip bands of undissociated dislocations. Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
